newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Sainsbury eyes stable margins.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Sainsbury eyes stable margins.

text.p: British supermarket group J. Sainsbury Plc hopes to maintain stable margins after annual results which showed a profits dip but increased sales last year, chief executive Dino Adriano told Reuters in an interview.
"Our great hope is that we can at least achieve stable margins, we'd like to do better," he said.

Sainsbury turned in a fall in pre-tax profits before exceptional items of 15 percent to 651 million stg for the year ending March 8, slightly above its warnings in January, and paid out a dividend of 12.3 pence per share, compared with 12.1 pence.
The group said current same store sales were up 4.2 percent compared with a four percent gain in the 16 weeks to January 11.
"The tide has turned. Our like for like sales are rising while others are falling," Adriano said.
"With inflation at 1.5 (percent), that's real volume growth...of over 2.5 percent," Adriano said.
He said Sainsbury's Reward loyalty card and extra Reward points had had "a major impact" on sales along with the "huge emphasis" on product availability.
Adriano said although improving product availability had "cost us a bit in the short term, it's really paying off now."

Sainsbury said in a statement with its results that operating margins had decreased to 6.2 percent last year, partly caused by the launch of Reward and a fierce petrol price war, which together cost the supermarkets 38 million pounds.
Sainsbury estimated that Reward card was now used for 80 percent of sales and Adriano said the next step was to obtain new customers.

"What we are seeing predominantly is very high usage of our Reward card and higher spend by our existing customers...secondary shoppers are coming back to Sainsbury's in floods, our next major thrust is to get new ones," he said.
A new advertising campaign in the next few weeks will focus on "Fresh foods, fresh ideas."
Adriano said that the supermarket, striving to regain ground against market leader Tesco, had managed to gain sales momentum.

"We've got it going. We're not stopping at this point, we've got the new advertising campaign...a lot of other developments coming through...we intend to build, and build, on what we have clearly started," he said.
Adriano said Sainsbury's Bank, its joint venture with Bank of Scotland, would make losses in the first couple of years, but "we're very, very pleased with the start."
He said Sainsbury wanted to develop organically in Northern Ireland, where it has two sites opened already.
"Our whole approach is to develop organically...our objective is to get a target number of stores between 12 and 15," he said.
But he did not rule out "the odd store" being bought by the chain.

Sainsbury said that supply chain improvements should see cost savings of 50 million pounds over the next three years while work on converting computer software to cope with the date change in 2000 would cost the group 40 million pounds, with half incurred in the current year.
